# Testing for HTML Injection — Summary (WSTG-CLNT-03)

HTML injection is a type of injection vulnerability that occurs when a user is able to control an input point and is able to inject arbitrary HTML code into a vulnerable web page. This vulnerability can have many consequences, like disclosure of a user's session cookies that could be used to impersonate the victim, or, more generally, it can allow the attacker to modify the page content seen by the victims.

This vulnerability occurs when user input is not correctly sanitized and the output is not encoded. An injection allows the attacker to send a malicious HTML page to a victim. The targeted browser will not be able to distinguish (trust) legitimate parts from malicious parts of the page, and consequently will parse and execute the whole page in the victim's context.

There is a wide range of methods and attributes that could be used to render HTML content. If these methods are provided with an untrusted input, then there is an high risk of HTML injection vulnerability. # HTML Injection Tutorial for Bug Bounty Hunters

## What it is
HTML injection is a type of vulnerability that lets attackers insert harmful HTML code into a website. When a user inputs data that isn't properly checked, the website might display this data directly, allowing an attacker to inject malicious HTML [1].

## Why it happens
This vulnerability occurs because the server doesn't sanitize user inputs before displaying them. If a user can control an input point and inject arbitrary HTML code, the browser won't be able to tell the difference between legitimate and malicious parts of the page, leading to potential attacks [1].

## How to find it
To find HTML injection vulnerabilities, look for places where user input is displayed without proper sanitization. Check if the application uses methods like `innerHTML` to render user-generated content. Also, examine how the application handles different types of input, such as URLs or form submissions, to see if they are processed securely [1, 3].

## A worked example
In one case, an attacker found an HTML injection vulnerability that allowed them to inject arbitrary HTML code into a web page. By manipulating the URL hash, the attacker was able to inject malicious HTML code that could alter the page content seen by other users [3].

## How to test it safely
When testing for HTML injection, ensure you are working within a controlled environment like a lab or on a target explicitly in scope for a bug bounty program you are authorized to test. Never perform tests on systems without permission.

## Key takeaways
- HTML injection occurs when user inputs are not sanitized and displayed directly on a webpage [1].
- Attackers can use this vulnerability to inject malicious HTML code, potentially altering page content or stealing sensitive information [1].
- To find HTML injection vulnerabilities, check how user inputs are handled and rendered on the page [1, 3].

# Testing for Host Header Injection — How to Test (WSTG-INPV-17)

Initial testing is as simple as supplying another domain (i.e. `attacker.com`) into the Host header field. It is how the web server processes the header value that dictates the impact. The attack is valid when the web server processes the input to send the request to an attacker-controlled host that resides at the supplied domain, and not to an internal virtual host that resides on the web server.

```http
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.attacker.com
[...]
```

In the simplest case, this may cause a 302 redirect to the supplied domain.

```http
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
[...]
Location: https://www.attacker.com/login.php

```

Alternatively, the web server may send the request to the first virtual host on the list.

### X-Forwarded Host Header Bypass

In the event that Host header injection is mitigated by checking for invalid input injected via the Host header, you can supply the value to the `X-Forwarded-Host` header.

```http
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-Forwarded-Host: www.attacker.com
[...]
```

[...]
<link src="https://www.attacker.com/link" />
[...]

# Testing for Host Header Injection — Summary (WSTG-INPV-17)

A web server commonly hosts several web applications on the same IP address, referring to each application via the virtual host. In an incoming HTTP request, web servers often dispatch the request to the target virtual host based on the value supplied in the Host header. Without proper validation of the header value, the attacker can supply invalid input to cause the web server to:

- Dispatch requests to the first virtual host on the list.
- Perform a redirect to an attacker-controlled domain.
- Perform web cache poisoning.
- Manipulate password reset functionality.
- Allow access to virtual hosts that were not intended to be externally accessible.

tutorial:
# Host Header Injection Tutorial

## What it is
Host header injection is a type of vulnerability that allows attackers to manipulate the Host header in HTTP requests to trick a web server into sending requests to an attacker-controlled domain instead of the intended one [1].

## Why it happens
This vulnerability occurs because web servers use the Host header to determine which virtual host to serve content from. If the server does not properly validate the Host header, an attacker can inject a malicious domain name, causing the server to send requests to that domain [1, 3].

## How to find it
To test for host header injection, start by sending a request with a custom Host header pointing to a domain you control. If the server redirects to your domain or sends requests to it, you have found a potential vulnerability [1]. Additionally, if the server mitigates Host header injection by validating input, try using the `X-Forwarded-Host` header instead [1].

## A worked example
Ahmed Hassan discovered a host header injection vulnerability in the United Nations' system. By injecting a malicious Host header, he was able to redirect the server to an attacker-controlled domain, leading to a full account takeover [2].

## How to test it safely
Testing for host header injection should be done in a controlled environment, such as a lab setup or on a target explicitly in scope for a bug bounty program you are authorized to test. Ensure you have permission before attempting any tests on live systems.

## Key takeaways
- Web servers use the Host header to route requests to specific virtual hosts [1].
- An attacker can exploit this by injecting a malicious domain name into the Host header [1].
- Proper validation of the Host header is crucial to prevent redirection to attacker-controlled domains [1].

# Testing for Session Fixation — Summary (WSTG-SESS-03)

Session fixation is enabled by the insecure practice of preserving the same value of the session cookies before and after authentication. This typically happens when session cookies are used to store state information even before login, e.g., to add items to a shopping cart before authenticating for payment.

In the generic exploit of session fixation vulnerabilities, an attacker can obtain a set of session cookies from the target site without first authenticating. The attacker can then force these cookies into the victim's browser using different techniques. If the victim later authenticates at the target site and the cookies are not refreshed upon login, the victim will be identified by the session cookies chosen by the attacker. The attacker is then able to impersonate the victim with these known cookies.

This issue can be fixed by refreshing the session cookies after the authentication process. Alternatively, the attack can be prevented by ensuring the integrity of session cookies. When considering network attackers, i.e., attackers who control the network used by the victim, use full [HSTS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki

sources.title: CWE-384: Session Fixation
sources.text:
# CWE-384: Session Fixation

Authenticating a user, or otherwise establishing a new user session, without invalidating any existing session identifier gives an attacker the opportunity to steal authenticated sessions.

Such a scenario is commonly observed when: A web application authenticates a user without first invalidating the existing session, thereby continuing to use the session already associated with the user. An attacker is able to force a known session identifier on a user so that, once the user authenticates, the attacker has access to the authenticated session. The application or container uses predictable session identifiers. In the generic exploit of session fixation vulnerabilities, an attacker creates a new session on a web application and records the associated session identifier. The attacker then causes the victim to associate, and possibly authenticate, against the server using that session identifier, giving the attacker access to the user's account through the active session.

**Applicable platforms:** Not Language-Specific, Web Based, Web Server

## Impact
- Access Control: Gain Privileges or Assume Identity

# Carriage Return Line Feed — Methodology

HTTP Response Splitting is a security vulnerability where an attacker manipulates an HTTP response by injecting Carriage Return (CR) and Line Feed (LF) characters (collectively called CRLF) into a response header. These characters mark the end of a header and the start of a new line in HTTP responses.

**CRLF Characters**:

* `CR` (`\r`, ASCII 13): Moves the cursor to the beginning of the line.
* `LF` (`\n`, ASCII 10): Moves the cursor to the next line.

By injecting a CRLF sequence, the attacker can break the response into two parts, effectively controlling the structure of the HTTP response. This can result in various security issues, such as:

* Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): Injecting malicious scripts into the second response.
* Cache Poisoning: Forcing incorrect content to be stored in caches.
* Header Manipulation: Altering headers to mislead users or systems

### Session Fixation

A typical HTTP response header looks like this:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Set-Cookie: sessionid=abc123
```

tutorial:
# Session Fixation Tutorial

## What it is
Session fixation is a type of attack where an attacker tricks a user into using a specific session identifier, allowing the attacker to hijack the user's session after the user logs in [1].

## Why it happens
The underlying flaw is that some applications do not change the session identifier after a user logs in. This means that if an attacker can get a user to log in with a session identifier the attacker already knows, the attacker can use that identifier to impersonate the user [1, 2].

## How to find it
To find session fixation vulnerabilities, observe if the session identifier remains unchanged after a user logs in. You can check this by logging in and examining the session cookies before and after authentication [1, 3].

## A worked example
An attacker can create a session on a website and note the session identifier. They can then trick a victim into using this session identifier by sending them a link with the session identifier embedded in it. Once the victim logs in, the attacker can use the known session identifier to access the victim's account [5].

## How to test it safely
Testing for session fixation should be done in a controlled environment, such as a lab or on a target explicitly in scope for a program you are authorized to test. Ensure you have permission to test the system and follow ethical guidelines to avoid causing harm.

## Key takeaways
- Always ensure session identifiers are refreshed after a user logs in [1, 6].
- Check if session identifiers remain the same before and after authentication [1, 3].
- Prevent session fixation by invalidating old session identifiers during login [6].

The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is used to store information about users, hosts, and many other objects. [LDAP injection](https://wiki.owasp.org/index.php/LDAP_injection) is a server-side attack, which could allow sensitive information about users and hosts represented in an LDAP structure to be disclosed, modified, or inserted. sources.title: LDAP Injection
sources.text:
# LDAP Injection — Methodology

LDAP Injection is a vulnerability that occurs when user-supplied input is used to construct LDAP queries without proper sanitization or escaping

### Authentication Bypass

Attempt to manipulate the filter logic by injecting always-true conditions.

**Example 1**: This LDAP query exploits logical operators in the query structure to potentially bypass authentication

```sql
user  = *)(uid=*))(|(uid=*
pass  = password
query = (&(uid=*)(uid=*))(|(uid=*)(userPassword={MD5}X03MO1qnZdYdgyfeuILPmQ==))
```

**Example 2**: This LDAP query exploits logical operators in the query structure to potentially bypass authentication

```sql
user  = admin)(!(&(1=0
pass  = q))
query = (&(uid=admin)(!(&(1=0)(userPassword=q))))
```

### Blind Exploitation

This scenario demonstrates LDAP blind exploitation using a technique similar to binary search or character-based brute-forcing to discover sensitive information like passwords. It relies on the fact that LDAP filters respond differently to queries based on whether the conditions match or not, without directly revealing the actual password.

sources.text:
# CAPEC-136: LDAP Injection

An attacker manipulates or crafts an LDAP query for the purpose of undermining the security of the target. Some applications use user input to create LDAP queries that are processed by an LDAP server. For example, a user might provide their username during authentication and the username might be inserted in an LDAP query during the authentication process. An attacker could use this input to inject additional commands into an LDAP query that could disclose sensitive information. For example, entering a * in the aforementioned query might return information about all users on the system. This attack is very similar to an SQL injection attack in that it manipulates a query to gather additional information or coerce a particular return value.

**likelihood of attack: High | typical severity: High | minimum skill: Medium**

## Prerequisites
- The target application must accept a string as user input, fail to sanitize characters that have a special meaning in LDAP queries in the user input, and insert the user-supplied string in an LDAP query which is then processed.

tutorial:
# LDAP Injection Tutorial for Bug Bounty Hunters

## What it is
LDAP Injection is an attack where an attacker manipulates user input to alter LDAP queries, leading to unauthorized access or information disclosure [1].

## Why it happens
It happens because web applications improperly handle user input when constructing LDAP queries, allowing attackers to inject malicious content that can change the query's logic [1, 2].

## How to find it
To find LDAP injection vulnerabilities, look for places where user input is directly included in LDAP queries without proper sanitization. Test by injecting special characters and logical operators to see if they affect the query's outcome [1, 2].

## A worked example
Consider an authentication mechanism that uses LDAP queries to validate user credentials. By injecting `*)(uid=*))(|(uid=*`, an attacker can bypass authentication by forcing the query to always return true, regardless of the actual user credentials [1].

## How to test it safely
Testing for LDAP injection should be done in a controlled environment such as a lab or on targets explicitly authorized for testing within a bug bounty program. Ensure you have permission before attempting any tests.

## Key takeaways
- LDAP Injection occurs when user input is improperly sanitized in LDAP queries [1].
- Attackers can manipulate LDAP queries to bypass authentication or retrieve sensitive information [1, 2].
- Properly sanitize and escape user inputs to prevent LDAP Injection [1].

sources.text:
# Testing for XPath Injection — Summary (WSTG-INPV-09)

XPath is a language that has been designed and developed primarily to address parts of an XML document. In XPath injection testing, we test if it is possible to inject XPath syntax into a request interpreted by the application, allowing an attacker to execute user-controlled XPath queries. When successfully exploited, this vulnerability may allow an attacker to bypass authentication mechanisms or access information without proper authorization.

Web applications heavily use databases to store and access the data they need for their operations. Historically, relational databases have been by far the most common technology for data storage, but, in the last years, we are witnessing an increasing popularity for databases that organize data using the XML language. Just like relational databases are accessed via SQL language, XML databases use XPath as their standard query language.

sources.title: CAPEC-83: XPath Injection
sources.text:
# CAPEC-83: XPath Injection

An attacker can craft special user-controllable input consisting of XPath expressions to inject the XML database and bypass authentication or glean information that they normally would not be able to. XPath Injection enables an attacker to talk directly to the XML database, thus bypassing the application completely. XPath Injection results from the failure of an application to properly sanitize input used as part of dynamic XPath expressions used to query an XML database.

**likelihood of attack: High | typical severity: High | minimum skill: Low**

## Prerequisites
- XPath queries used to retrieve information stored in XML documents
- User-controllable input not properly sanitized before being used as part of XPath queries

sources.title: Testing for XPath Injection
sources.text: Since, from a conceptual point of view, XPath is very similar to SQL in its purpose and applications, an interesting result is that XPath injection attacks follow the same logic as [SQL Injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/SQL_Injection) attacks. In some aspects, XPath is even more powerful than standard SQL, as its whole power is already present in its specifications, whereas a large number of the techniques that can be used in a SQL Injection attack depend on the characteristics of the SQL dialect used by the target database. This means that XPath injection attacks can be much more adaptable and ubiquitous. Another advantage of an XPath injection attack is that, unlike SQL, no ACLs are enforced, as our query can access every part of the XML document.

sources.text:
# CWE-643: Improper Neutralization of Data within XPath Expressions ('XPath Injection')

The product uses external input to dynamically construct an XPath expression used to retrieve data from an XML database, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes that input. This allows an attacker to control the structure of the query.

The net effect is that the attacker will have control over the information selected from the XML database and may use that ability to control application flow, modify logic, retrieve unauthorized data, or bypass important checks (e.g. authentication).

**Likelihood of exploit:** High

# XPath Injection Tutorial for Bug Bounty Hunters

## What it is
XPath injection is a type of attack where an attacker injects malicious XPath syntax into a web application’s input fields. This allows the attacker to manipulate the application's queries to an XML database, potentially leading to unauthorized access or data retrieval [1].

## Why it happens
This vulnerability occurs because the application fails to properly sanitize user inputs before using them in XPath queries. As a result, attackers can inject harmful code that alters the intended query, leading to security breaches [2].

## How to find it
To identify XPath injection vulnerabilities, look for places where user input is directly used in XPath queries without proper validation or sanitization. Common entry points include search forms, login pages, and other interactive elements that accept user input [1, 2].

## A worked example
Consider a login page that uses an XML database to authenticate users. The application constructs an XPath query to verify credentials based on user input. If the application does not sanitize the input, an attacker can inject a crafted string such as `' or '1' = '1` into both the username and password fields. This would alter the query to always return true, effectively bypassing authentication [4].

## How to test it safely
When testing for XPath injection, ensure you are authorized to do so on the target system. Use a controlled environment like a lab or a target explicitly in scope for a bug bounty program. Start by injecting simple payloads to observe how the application handles unexpected input. Gradually increase complexity to understand the extent of the vulnerability [4].

## Key takeaways
- XPath injection exploits occur when user inputs are improperly sanitized before being used in XPath queries [2].
- Attackers can use this vulnerability to bypass authentication mechanisms or access sensitive data [1].
- Testing should be conducted in a safe, authorized environment to avoid causing harm or legal issues [4].

# CAPEC-134: Email Injection

An adversary manipulates the headers and content of an email message by injecting data via the use of delimiter characters native to the protocol.

Many applications allow users to send email messages by filling in fields. For example, a web site may have a link to "share this site with a friend" where the user provides the recipient's email address and the web application fills out all the other fields, such as the subject and body. In this pattern, an adversary adds header and body information to an email message by injecting additional content in an input field used to construct a header of the mail message. This attack takes advantage of the fact that RFC 822 requires that headers in a mail message be separated by a carriage return. As a result, an adversary can inject new headers or content simply by adding a delimiting carriage return and then supplying the new heading and body information. This attack will not work if the user can only supply the message body since a carriage return in the body is treated as a normal character.

# Email Header Injection Tutorial

## What it is
Email header injection is a technique where an attacker manipulates the headers and content of an email message by injecting data through the use of delimiter characters native to the email protocol [1].

## Why it happens
This vulnerability occurs because many applications allow users to send email messages by filling in fields. When constructing an email, if the application improperly handles user inputs, an attacker can inject additional headers or content by adding a carriage return followed by new header or body information [1].

## How to find it
To identify email header injection vulnerabilities, look for web forms or APIs that allow users to send emails. Test these interfaces by inserting newline characters (`\r\n`) followed by additional headers or content. If the application constructs the email incorrectly, it may include the injected content [1, 3].

## A worked example
In one instance, an attacker exploited a webmail application to inject malicious email headers. By sending crafted emails with headers containing metacharacter-based payloads, the attacker determined how the application processed the malicious content. This allowed the attacker to inject headers that caused the email client to behave unexpectedly [3].

## How to test it safely
Testing for email header injection should be done in a controlled environment, such as a lab setup, or on a target explicitly in scope for a bug bounty program you are authorized to test. Ensure that you have permission before attempting any tests on live systems.

## Key takeaways
- Email header injection occurs when an application improperly handles user inputs in email construction [1].
- Attackers can inject additional headers or content by using delimiter characters [1].
- Testing involves inserting newline characters and observing if the application includes the injected content [3].

# Tutorial: Understanding and Finding Integer Overflows in Bug Bounty Hunting

## What it is
An integer overflow happens when a calculation produces a result that is too large to fit into the space reserved for it, causing the value to wrap around to a smaller or negative number [1].

## Why it happens
This issue arises because the programmer did not account for the maximum possible value an integer can hold. When an integer reaches its maximum limit and is incremented further, it resets to a very small or negative number, leading to unexpected behavior [1].

## How to find it
To identify integer overflows, look for places where calculations are performed on integers without proper checks for overflow conditions. Tools like SAST (Static Application Security Testing) can help by analyzing the code for potential vulnerabilities [3]. Additionally, dynamic analysis tools that check for memory safety issues can also be useful [3].

## A worked example
In the VLC media player, an integer overflow was found in the VNC module. This vulnerability could lead to memory corruption, allowing attackers to manipulate memory in ways unintended by the developers [2].

## How to test it safely
Testing for integer overflows should be done in a controlled environment, such as a lab setup or on targets that are explicitly within the scope of a bug bounty program you have authorization to test. Never attempt to exploit vulnerabilities on systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

## Key takeaways
- Integer overflows happen when calculations exceed the maximum value an integer can hold [1].
- Look for unguarded arithmetic operations involving integers [1].
- Use static and dynamic analysis tools to detect potential integer overflow vulnerabilities [3].

# Race Condition — Methodology

### Limit-overrun

Limit-overrun refers to a scenario where multiple threads or processes compete to update or access a shared resource, resulting in the resource exceeding its intended limits.

**Examples**: Overdrawing limit, multiple voting, multiple spending of a giftcard.

- [Race Condition allows to redeem multiple times gift cards which leads to free "money" - @muon4](https://hackerone.com/reports/759247)
- [Race conditions can be used to bypass invitation limit - @franjkovic](https://hackerone.com/reports/115007)
- [Register multiple users using one invitation - @franjkovic](https://hackerone.com/reports/148609)

### Rate-limit Bypass

Rate-limit bypass occurs when an attacker exploits the lack of proper synchronization in rate-limiting mechanisms to exceed intended request limits. Rate-limiting is designed to control the frequency of actions (e.g., API requests, login attempts), but race conditions can allow attackers to bypass these restrictions.

**Examples**: Bypassing anti-bruteforce mechanism and 2FA.

# Missing Rate Limiting

## What it is
Missing rate limiting means there are no restrictions on how many times a user can perform certain actions, such as sending password reset emails or requesting one-time passwords (OTPs). This allows attackers to repeatedly try actions until they succeed [1].

## Why it happens
This issue arises because developers often forget to implement safeguards that limit the frequency of specific actions. Without rate limiting, systems can be overwhelmed by repeated requests, leading to vulnerabilities like brute force attacks [1, 3].

## How to find it
To find missing rate limiting, look for areas where users can repeatedly trigger actions without waiting periods. Common targets include password reset pages, OTP request forms, and other sensitive operations. Test these areas by making numerous requests in quick succession to see if the system imposes any limits [1, 3].

## A worked example
In one instance, a researcher found that Facebook allowed unlimited attempts to add unowned phone numbers to accounts due to missing rate limiting. By repeatedly sending requests, the researcher could bypass the system’s checks and add any phone number [1].

## How to test it safely
Testing for missing rate limiting should always be done in a controlled environment or on targets explicitly authorized for testing. Never abuse the vulnerability by causing denial of service or other harmful effects. Ensure you have permission before testing any system [no citation needed].

## Key takeaways
- Missing rate limiting lets attackers repeatedly attempt actions without restriction [1].
- Developers often overlook implementing rate limiting, leading to vulnerabilities [1, 3].
- Testing involves making multiple requests to see if the system enforces any limits [1, 3].

# Insecure Cookie Flags

## What it is

Insecure cookie flags refer to missing or improperly set attributes on cookies that are critical for maintaining the security of a web application's session management. These flags include the `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, and `SameSite` attributes, each serving a specific purpose to protect against various types of attacks [1, 3].

## Why it happens

The underlying flaw is often due to developers forgetting to set these important flags or misunderstanding their significance. For example, the `Secure` flag ensures that cookies are only sent over HTTPS connections, preventing them from being intercepted over unsecured HTTP connections [3]. Similarly, the `HttpOnly` flag prevents JavaScript from accessing the cookie, reducing the risk of session hijacking through XSS attacks [4]. Lastly, the `SameSite` attribute helps mitigate CSRF attacks by controlling how cookies are sent with cross-site requests [6].

## How to find it

To identify insecure cookie flags, start by inspecting the cookies sent by the web application using developer tools in your browser. Look for cookies that are critical for session management and check if they have the `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, and `SameSite` flags set appropriately. You can also use automated tools designed for security testing to scan for these issues [3].

## A worked example

One real case involves a web application that did not set the `Secure` flag on a cookie containing sensitive information. As a result, the cookie was sent over both HTTP and HTTPS connections, making it vulnerable to interception over unsecured HTTP connections [3].

## How to test it safely

This type of testing should be conducted in a controlled environment such as a lab or on a target explicitly in scope for a program you are authorized to test. Ensure you have permission before testing any live systems.

## Key takeaways

- Set the `Secure` flag on all cookies that contain sensitive information to ensure they are only transmitted over HTTPS [3].
- Enable the `HttpOnly` flag on cookies to prevent JavaScript from accessing them, reducing the risk of session hijacking through XSS attacks [4].
- Configure the `SameSite` attribute properly to mitigate CSRF attacks by controlling how cookies are sent with cross-site requests [6].

> Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)  is a vulnerability that arises when an attacker can inject malicious input into a server-side template, causing arbitrary code execution on the server. In Python, SSTI can occur when using templating engines such as Jinja2, Mako, or Django templates, where user input is included in templates without proper sanitization.

# Server Side Template Injection - Java

> Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)  is a security vulnerability that occurs when user input is embedded into server-side templates in an unsafe manner, allowing attackers to inject and execute arbitrary code. In Java, SSTI can be particularly dangerous due to the power and flexibility of Java-based templating engines such as JSP (JavaServer Pages), Thymeleaf, and FreeMarker.

# Server Side Include Injection — Methodology

SSI Injection occurs when an attacker can input Server Side Include directives into a web application. SSIs are directives that can include files, execute commands, or print environment variables/attributes. If user input is not properly sanitized within an SSI context, this input can be used to manipulate server-side behavior and access sensitive information or execute commands.

SSI format: `<!--#directive param="value" -->`

> Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)  is a class of vulnerabilities where an attacker can inject malicious input into a server-side template, causing the template engine to execute arbitrary code on the server. # Server-side Include Injection

## What it is
Server-side include injection (SSI injection) is a type of vulnerability where an attacker can input Server Side Include directives into a web application. These directives can include files, execute commands, or print environment variables/attributes [4].

## Why it happens
This vulnerability happens because user input is not properly sanitized within an SSI context. When user input is allowed to be part of an SSI directive, it can be manipulated to change server-side behavior, leading to unauthorized actions [4].

## How to find it
To find SSI injection vulnerabilities, look for places where user input is reflected in the response. Check if the application uses SSI directives like `<!--#include file="user_input"-->` or similar constructs. Try injecting common SSI directives to see if they are executed [4].

## A worked example
An example of SSI injection can be seen in a scenario where a web application includes user input in an SSI directive without proper sanitization. For instance, if a page includes a file based on user input like `<!--#include file="/path/to/user_input"-->`, an attacker could inject a path to a sensitive file, such as `/etc/passwd`, to read its contents [4].

## How to test it safely
Testing for SSI injection should be done in a controlled environment, such as a lab setup or on a target explicitly in scope for a program you are authorized to test. Ensure you have permission before testing any live systems.

## Key takeaways
- SSI injection allows attackers to manipulate server-side behavior by injecting directives.
- It occurs when user input is not properly sanitized within SSI contexts.
- Look for places where user input is reflected in SSI directives to identify potential vulnerabilities.
